title: Mass schooling and literacy
summary: Prussia's decree of 1763 ordered children to school from age five until thirteen or fourteen. Two centuries ago, the best estimate is that 12% of the world's people could read and write. Global literacy more than doubled over the 19th century, and more than four out of five people can now read. Literacy improved especially fast in northwest Europe in 1600–1800, and by the mid-19th century, school enrollment in the United States exceeded that of any other nation.

as_recorded.value: 12% of the world population was literate
By the mid-nineteenth century school enrollment rates in the United States exceeded those of any other nation

where.modern_name: Worldwide; stand-in pin at Berlin, Germany

importance.justification: Reading went from a skill of a small elite to one held by most people.

related.because: Movable-type printing dramatically lowered the cost of books, providing the reading materials essential for widespread literacy.
